qAndA.answer: Deimos's orbit is slowly widening, causing it to move away from Mars over time, unlike Phobos, which is on a decaying orbit, drawing it closer to the planet.

videoEditingDetails.description: Cut to a space scene featuring the Moon and a spacecraft.
Text overlay: 'It may never happen to our moon, but Mars has some unique examples.'
Cut to a view of Mars and its two moons, Phobos and Deimos.
Text overlay: 'Phobos and Deimos are two asteroid-like moons that orbit the red planet in different ways.'
Cut to a closer view of Phobos orbiting Mars.
Text overlay: 'Phobos is the larger of the two with an extremely close orbit to Mars. That inches closer and closer every year, culminating to six feet closer every century.'

Text overlay: 'There are already places on Mars's surface where Phobos cannot be seen due to how closely it hugs in orbit.'

Cut to a view of Deimos in space.
Text overlay: 'Deimos is smaller in comparison with an orbit that is slowly widening, leading to it doing the opposite and eventually flying off into space.'

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: What happens when a moon is thrown out of orbit? It may never happen to our
moon, but Mars has some unique examples. Fobos and Deimos are two asteroid-like
moons that orbit the red planet in different ways. Fobos is the larger of the
two with an extremely close orbit to Mars that inches closer and closer
every year, culminating to six feet closer every century. There are already
places on Mars's surface where Fobos cannot be seen due to how closely it
hugs in orbit. It will eventually crash into Mars or crumble apart due to
tidal forces in around 50 million years. Deimos is smaller in comparison with an
orbit that is slowly widening, leading to it doing the opposite and eventually
flying off into space. Moons like these are a good example of all the possible
planetary scenarios playing out in the vastness of space.

youtube_description:
Ever wondered about moons on the move? Mars has unique examples – Phobos inching closer each century and Deimos gradually drifting away.

Phobos, the larger moon, nears Mars, and it's expected to crash or crumble in 50 million years. Meanwhile, smaller Deimos widens its orbit, eventually drifting off.

Planetary scenarios unfold in space! What do you think about these Martian moons?
